awd_titl_txt: Conference: Methane Alert: What measurement framework is needed to monitor increasing natural methane emissions?
awd_abstract_narration:
This award will fund a workshop in October, 2025 at the Aspen Global Change Institute to review the available fundamental science of increasing natural methane emissions and assess potential frameworks, strategies, and thresholds for further monitoring and mitigation. This workshop will convene approximately thirty participants for a weeklong program of technical presentations, discussions, working groups, and opportunities for public engagement. Workshop participants will represent a range of disciplines, issue areas, geographies, and types of expertise including climate modeling, methane detection and monitoring (ground-based, aerial, and satellite observations), biogeochemical observations, ecology, and risk management.

Key goals of the workshop are to: i) synthesize available evidence of increasing natural methane emissions; ii) evaluate potential risks and consequences of unmonitored natural methane emissions;  and iii) consider research needs and collaboration opportunities for developing and deploying a framework to study positive feedbacks. The workshop will increase collaboration across research disciplines and geographies that have not had other venues to connect on this issue, to evaluate current gaps in the capacity to monitor, model, and anticipate these emission increases. Participants also will will engage the public through a lecture, as well as web-accessible videos of workshop proceedings.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The scope of the effort was designed to enable an innovative analysis of natural methane emissions, how we manage risks in the system today and how we might consider adjusting our strategy in the future. It was our hope from the outset that workshop outcomes would inform future monitoring efforts to expand into areas that currently have sparse coverage yet represent some of the greatest risks for increased emissions. 

In so doing, our overarching goal was to reduce the risk posed by rising natural methane emissions to the global community. In addition to expanding and strengthening collaboration across disciplines and geographies and bringing attention to a critically under-studied area of the climate system, we also anticipated a peer reviewed publication of the workshop findings. In addition, AGCI aimed to engage the public on the societal relevance of this topic through a public lecture and the public dissemination of educational materials. 

All of these initial aims were achieved, with clear lessons identified for science and funding communities to carry forward the work in ways that will continue to advance scientific understanding, mitigate risks in the future, and engage the public on this topic. 

Recommendations for the Scientific Community
The workshop identified several priorities that would substantially improve understanding of natural methane emissions and accelerate development of an integrated global measurement framework.

  • Expand observations in priority ecosystems: Continue strategic expansion of long-term observations across both high-latitude and tropical ecosystems, with particular emphasis on improving representativeness in regions that remain under-observed. 
  • Integrate observations across spatial scales: Develop coordinated observing strategies that intentionally connect chamber measurements, eddy covariance towers, atmospheric monitoring stations, aircraft campaigns, satellite observations, isotopic measurements, and Earth system models. 
  • Improve attribution and data integration: Strengthen methods for integrating top-down and bottom-up observations, improving atmospheric inversions, advancing isotopic analyses, and combining diverse datasets through data assimilation and machine learning. Reducing uncertainty in source attribution remains one of the highest scientific priorities identified during the workshop.
  • Strengthen long-term observing networks: Support sustained observations capable of detecting long-term trends, episodic emission events, and ecosystem responses to climate variability and change. Long-term continuity is essential for distinguishing transient variability from persistent climate-driven changes.
  • Promote interoperability and open science: Develop common measurement protocols, metadata standards, quality assurance practices, and interoperable data products that facilitate synthesis across observing networks and scientific disciplines.
  • Foster interdisciplinary collaboration: Continue building partnerships among atmospheric scientists, ecologists, hydrologists, remote sensing experts, modelers, and data scientists. 


Funding Recommendations
Participants identified several areas where funding organizations can play a unique catalytic role by complementing existing government investments and accelerating scientific coordination.

  • Support observations in underrepresented regions: Strategic investments can help establish or expand long-term monitoring in tropical wetlands, high-latitude ecosystems, and inland waters where scientific uncertainty remains greatest and traditional funding mechanisms are limited.
  • Invest in coordination and integration: Many of the components of an integrated methane measurement framework already exist. Philanthropic funding can help connect these efforts by supporting data integration, collaborative synthesis activities, cross-network coordination, and interdisciplinary working groups.
  • Build regional scientific capacity: Support long-term partnerships with regional institutions, local scientists, and Indigenous communities through training, workforce development, infrastructure, and collaborative research. 
  • Support community-building activities: Continue investing in workshops, collaborative networks, synthesis efforts, and open data initiatives that bring together researchers across disciplines and regions. 


Early Impacts of the Workshop
As of summer 2026, the workshop has already contributed to multiple publications that articulate the scientific rationale and vision for a coordinated global methane observing system. 

Publications: 
Watts, Jennifer D., et al. 2026. "A global methane observation system to track climate feedbacks for verifiable climate impact." Science 391.6792 (2026): 1324-1327. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aef0459
This Science Policy Forum article outlines the scientific rationale for developing a coordinated global methane observation system capable of detecting and attributing changes in both anthropogenic and natural methane emissions. 


Ciais, P.,  et al., 2026. "A global methane observation system to reduce uncertainty for anthropogenic and natural sources and sinks for detecting and attributing climate feedbacks.”  Advanced Science.  Accepted.  
This research article expands on the workshop discussions by presenting a vision for an integrated methane measurement framework that combines atmospheric observations, ecosystem measurements, remote sensing, and Earth system modeling to improve understanding of methane sources, sinks, and climate feedbacks. 

Notably, the workshop also spurred new philanthropic investment (~$2.7M) to address sparse monitoring, by deploying 5 EM27/SUN instruments across Africa through collaboration among UCLA, NASA, Spark Climate Solutions, LSCE, and University of Edinburgh, and 5 host African institutions.

The workshop also engaged the public on this topic through a public lecture entitled, "Measuring Methane in the Arctic: Training the Next Generation of Researchers Through Fieldwork," by Ruth Varner (University of New Hampshire), as well as the posting of all workshop talks on the workshop website as educational resources.
